 Congresswoman Grace Meng Reintroduces Bill To Make Diwali A Federal Holiday
 News November 9, 2026 indica 
 Share the news iNDICA NEWS BUREAU- 
 A renewed push to recognize Diwali as a federal holiday in the U.S. has gained support from lawmakers, with Congresswoman Grace Meng reintroducing legislation that would add the Hindu festival of lights to the country’s official holiday calendar.
 The proposed Diwali Day Act seeks to make Diwali the 12th federal holiday in the U.S.
 Meng said the move would recognize the contributions of Hindu, Sikh, Jain and Buddhist communities while sending a message of inclusion at a time of growing concerns over religious and ethnic hate.
 Meng, who chairs the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC), said recognizing Diwali would help affirm the place of these communities in American society.
 “Diwali represents the triumph of good over evil and knowledge over ignorance,” she said.
 This Diwali, I’m wishing everyone celebrating in Queens and beyond joy, prosperity, and light.
 My Diwali Day Act would make this joyous holiday a federal holiday—recognition that is long overdue.
 The racist, anti-Hindu disruption in Seattle stands against the spirit of Diwali. Everyone deserves to celebrate safely and freely. We must stand together against this bigotry and hate in all its forms.
 May light triumph over darkness, and hope over hate.
 — Grace Meng (@RepGraceMeng) November 8, 2026 
 The legislation has 19 co-sponsors, including Indian-American lawmakers Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Raja Krishnamoorthi, Suhas Subramanyam and Shri Thanedar.
 Other lawmakers backing the bill include Nanette Barragán, Wesley Bell, André Carson, Judy Chu, Suzan DelBene, Josh Gottheimer, Timothy Kennedy, Stephen Lynch, Deborah Ross, Lateefah Simon, Tom Suozzi, Mark Takano, Rashida Tlaib and Bonnie Watson Coleman.
 Meng said federal recognition of Diwali was particularly important amid concerns about anti-Hindu and anti-South Asian hate.
 “At a time when anti-Hindu and anti-South Asian hate is on the rise, recognizing Diwali as a federal holiday sends a powerful message that Hindus, as well as Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists, are valued members of our society,” Meng said.
 The bill proposes an amendment to Section 6103(a) of Title 5 of the U.S. Code to include Diwali Day in the list of legal public holidays. If passed, it would make Diwali the 12th federal holiday in the country, according to Meng’s announcement.
 Meng also pointed to her experience in Queens, New York, which has a large South Asian population, and said she had seen how important the festival was to local families and communities.
 “Here in Queens, I see firsthand how meaningful Diwali is to so many families and communities,” Meng said. “My Diwali Day Act will help educate Americans about the importance of this day, and I will continue working to create a more inclusive nation that honors the rich cultural traditions of its people.”
 CAPAC also linked the legislation to concerns about religious intimidation and attacks targeting Hindu and South Asian communities. Its announcement cited vandalism at Hindu places of worship, an alleged mass-shooting plot targeting a Hindu gathering in Illinois and the recent disruption of a Diwali celebration in Washington state.
 The caucus called for such incidents to be taken seriously and investigated by federal authorities. While its statement described anti-Hindu and anti-South Asian hate as rising, it did not provide statistical evidence to support the claim.
 Meng’s office said the legislation has received endorsements from 17 civil rights, religious and community organizations.
 The congresswoman said federal recognition would give communities more opportunities to celebrate Diwali and help Americans understand its cultural and religious significance. She has also separately proposed legislation to establish Lunar New Year as a federal holiday.
